content: The half-life of a quantity undergoing exponential decay is defined as the time required for the quantity to reduce to half of its initial value. This concept was originally developed in the context of radioactive decay but has since been applied to various other fields, including processes that do not strictly follow exponential decay patterns. The term half-life was first introduced in 1907, initially referred to as the half-life period. However, the word period was dropped from the terminology in the early 1950s. The reduction of a quantity over time, in terms of elapsed half-lives, can be mathematically described using the decay constant (λ), which is a positive constant that characterizes the rate of exponential decay. The half-life is mathematically related to the mean lifetime (τ) of the decaying substance. The decay constant (λ) can represent different physical quantities depending on the specific process being described. For example: In an RC or RL electrical circuit, λ is the reciprocal of the circuit's time constant. For simple RC and RL circuits, λ equals 1/RC or R/L, respectively. In first-order chemical reactions, λ corresponds to the reaction rate constant. In radioactive decay, λ represents the probability of decay per unit time, expressed as ( dN = lambda N dt ), where ( dN ) is the number of nuclei decayed during the time interval ( dt ), and ( N ) is the number of radioactive nuclei present. In pharmacokinetics, the half-life of a substance (such as a drug or radioactive nuclide) is the time it takes for the substance to lose half of its pharmacologic, physiologic, or radiologic activity. This concept was formally introduced in 1974, though it had been in use since 1971. Some quantities decay through multiple simultaneous processes. In such cases, the effective half-life is determined by the harmonic mean of the half-lives associated with each individual process. Quantities subject to exponential decay are often denoted by the symbol ( N ), which typically represents a decaying number of discrete items. The value of ( N ) at a given time ( t ) is described by the formula ( N(t) = N_0 e^{-lambda t} ), where ( N_0 ) is the initial value of ( N ) at ( t = 0 ). At ( t = 0 ), the exponential term equals 1, so ( N(t) = N_0 ). As ( t ) approaches infinity, the exponential term approaches zero. The half-life ( t_{1/2} ) is the time at which ( N(t) = N_0 / 2 ). The half-life of a process can be experimentally determined, even without prior knowledge of the decay law governing the process. This is particularly useful for validating the concept of half-life in radioactive decay, especially when dealing with a small number of atoms. Experiments and computer simulations are often employed to test the behavior of the last remaining atoms and to validate physics-mathematical models by comparing their predictions with experimental observations or valid simulations. In radioactive decay, the exponential model does not apply when the number of atoms is very small. This limitation arises because radioactive decay occurs in discrete units, meaning that after a sufficient number of half-lives, the remaining quantity of the original substance becomes exactly zero, rather than asymptotically approaching zero as in continuous systems. Simple experiments using pennies or M&M's candies can illustrate this concept. Similar experiments can be conducted with isotopes that have very short half-lives. Additionally, computer programs can be written to simulate radioactive decay, incorporating the required randomness, to observe the behavior of the last remaining atoms.
